title: Fuel information, then the purchase
hook: Does giving personalized fuel costs guarantee a different car purchase?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Distinguish an information treatment from evidence that the final choice changed.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Distinguish an information treatment from evidence that the final choice changed.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy shopper changes a fuel-cost estimate from thirty to forty-five but keeps choice id one. How many choice identifiers change? Toy inputs A=[30, 45, 1, 1]; B=[30, 45, 1, 0].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[15, 0, 1], [15, -1, 0]]. Labels: Estimate change, Choice change, Final choice.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: An information update and a purchase change are different outcomes. The comparison changes the chosen identifier, whereas the question case does not. Showing someone relevant numbers does not logically entail that their final choice must change.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Old cost estimate=30, New cost estimate=45, Old choice id=1, New choice id=0. What is Choice change? Answer: -1.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Old cost estimate=30, New cost estimate=45, Old choice id=1, New choice id=0. What is Choice change?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives -1. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.section: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceProvenance.text: Giving car shoppers personalized fuel-cost information did not change which cars they bought (Allcott & Knittel, 2019).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Distinguish an information treatment from evidence that the final choice changed.
